title: Medicine enters the university

confidence.note: Universities grew up gradually, so there is no single founding date; Montpellier's 1220 statutes and 1289 papal bull are documented. The 1322 case against Jacoba Felicie survives in the court records printed in the Paris university cartulary.

people: Cardinal Conrad, papal legate who gave Montpellier its 1220 statutes
Jacoba Felicie (fl. 1322), Paris healer prosecuted by the medical faculty
summary: In the 13th century medicine became a university degree, and the new doctors used their licenses to drive out rivals, including a skilled woman healer in Paris.
body: Medicine was one of the founding subjects of Europe's first universities. At Bologna the university grew out of student guilds; at Paris, by the late 12th century, a body of masters taught theology, law, medicine and arts. At Montpellier, statutes given in 1220 by the papal legate Cardinal Conrad placed the medical school under the bishop of Maguelonne, and a papal bull of 1289 joined its schools into a university. Students learned from books, above all Galen and Avicenna, the texts Pope Clement V prescribed for Montpellier in 1309, with anatomy taught from Mondino's manual.

Faculties used the license to police the market. In 1322 the Paris faculty prosecuted Jacoba Felicie, a woman of about thirty, for practicing without its approval, under a rule threatening excommunication and a fine of sixty Paris pounds. One patient testified that she had treated him better than the physicians would have. She argued that it was better and more decent for a skilled woman to examine a sick woman than for a man to do so. The same order named other unlicensed healers, among them a woman surgeon, Margaret of Ypres, and a Jewish woman, Belota.

title: Frederick II licenses doctors

confidence.note: The Constitutions of Melfi of 1231 survive and their medical clauses are well studied. How strictly the rules were enforced across the kingdom is much less clear.

people: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor and king of Sicily
summary: In 1231 Emperor Frederick II made medicine a regulated profession in southern Italy, with set studies, fee rules, and a wall between doctors and druggists.
body: In 1231, at Melfi, Emperor Frederick II issued a law code for his Kingdom of Sicily that devoted five constitutions to medicine. They fixed the course of study and the conditions for admission to practice, with the masters of Salerno at the center; William Osler summarized them as three years of preliminary study and five of medicine, surgery included. The laws set how often doctors should visit patients and what they could charge, and banned partnerships between physicians and apothecaries, who had to swear to make up prescriptions honestly. Surgeons needed proof of a year's study, including human anatomy.

title: The invention of spectacles

confidence.note: A sermon of 1306 and a Pisan convent chronicle put the invention a couple of decades earlier, and Venetian guild rules show eyeglasses in production by about 1300. The inventor is unknown; credit to Alessandro della Spina rests on the chronicle, which itself says he copied someone else.

people: Alessandro della Spina (d. 1313), Dominican friar of Pisa
summary: Around 1286 someone in northern Italy riveted two lenses together and gave aging readers back their eyes. Nobody knows who, and the famous name on a Florentine tomb is a hoax.
body: Eyeglasses appeared in northern Italy in the late 13th century, and no one knows who made the first pair. The evidence points to the years shortly after 1286, most likely in Pisa. In a sermon of 1306 the Dominican preacher Giordano da Pisa spoke of the new invention, and the chronicle of his Pisan convent of Santa Caterina credits his fellow friar Alessandro della Spina with making them around 1290, while admitting that Alessandro copied a pair from someone who had made them first and would not share the secret. By 1300 Venetian glassmakers were producing eyeglasses, and the city's guild rules mention them repeatedly over the next two decades.

The first spectacles were two convex lenses in frames riveted together at the handles, clamped on the nose and often steadied by hand. They helped the farsighted read, which suited the few who lived past their forties and could read at all. Lenses for the nearsighted, harder to grind, arrived only in the mid-15th century.

myth.tradition: Spectacles were invented by Salvino degli Armati of Florence, whose tomb in Santa Maria Maggiore called him the 'inventor of eyeglasses', and who got a monument there in the 19th century.
myth.record: The epitaph, supposedly dated 1318, first appears in Ferdinando Leopoldo del Migliore's 1684 history of Florence. The historian Isidoro del Lungo showed it to be a fabrication.

links.note: Earlier optics of lenses; Roger Bacon had described reading lenses.

title: Mondino dissects in Bologna

confidence.note: The Anathomia is dated 1316 in its own text and its use for two centuries is well documented. Whether Mondino wielded the knife himself or read while an assistant cut is still debated.

people: Mondino de' Liuzzi (c. 1275–1326), Bolognese physician and anatomist
summary: In 1316 a Bologna professor wrote the dissection manual that Europe's medical schools would read aloud over corpses for the next two centuries.
body: Bologna was already opening bodies before Mondino de' Liuzzi: from 1265 the city had physicians examine corpses in cases of fatal wounds. Mondino, a pupil of Taddeo Alderotti, made dissection part of teaching. In 1316 he finished his *Anathomia*, a short manual organized in the order a body has to be opened before it decays. He mentions anatomizing a woman in January 1316 and refers to dissections almost every month, on executed criminals and, it seems, the hospital poor. The book was used in Europe's medical schools until the mid-16th century.

Its anatomy was mostly Galen's and the Arabic writers', errors included: a five-lobed liver taken from dogs and a womb with seven chambers. It was written to be read aloud while others worked; in the scene later shown in printed editions a reader comments on the text, a demonstrator points, and a dissector cuts. Mondino could learn, though. By 1319, having read a new Latin translation of Galen's *On the Use of Parts*, he dropped the seven-chambered womb.

myth.tradition: Mondino's skilled assistant was a young woman, Alessandra Giliani, celebrated as the first female anatomist.
myth.record: The story was made up in 1739 by the Bolognese historian Alessandro Macchiavelli, who identified the long-haired dissector in a 15th-century woodcut as Alessandra and backed the claim with fake sources.

links.note: Mondino taught Galen's anatomy, mistakes and all.

title: The Black Death

confidence.note: Chronicles, tax records and burial grounds date the pandemic's spread across Europe closely, and ancient DNA has settled that the killer was Yersinia pestis. The death toll is an estimate from patchy records: recent studies quote anything from 30% to 60%, and the Central Asian origin rests on a single 2022 study of seven individuals.

place: Central Eurasia to Europe, the Middle East and North Africa
people: Maria Spyrou, geneticist, lead author of the 2022 origin study
Philip VI, king of France, who commissioned the Paris report
summary: Between 1346 and 1353 plague killed perhaps a third to more than half of the people it reached. Ancient DNA has now traced its source to tombstones by a lake in Kyrgyzstan.
body: In 1338 and 1339 a trading community near Lake Issyk-Kul, in what is now Kyrgyzstan, buried an unusual number of its dead under tombstones inscribed in Syriac. Some give the cause of death simply as "pestilence." In 2022 a team led by Maria Spyrou recovered plague DNA from the teeth of seven people excavated there in the 1880s. Their strain of *Yersinia pestis* sits at the exact root of the great branching of plague lineages linked to the pandemic's emergence, and its closest living relatives circulate among rodents in the Tian Shan mountains. The most popular earlier theory had placed the source in China.

By 1347 the disease had reached the Mediterranean on ships from the Golden Horde's ports on the Black Sea, and between 1346 and 1353 it swept through Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. How many died is still argued over: recent studies estimate 30 to 50% of the population, while others say up to 60%. For decades some scholars argued the killer was something other than plague, because medieval accounts did not match modern outbreaks. In 2010 DNA and proteins of *Yersinia pestis* were found in skeletons from plague pits in England, France, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, and a full medieval genome from a London cemetery followed in 2011.

People explained the catastrophe with the best science they had. In October 1348 the medical masters of Paris, asked by King Philip for a report, named a "distant and first cause": a conjunction of three planets in Aquarius at one hour after noon on 20 March 1345, which had corrupted the air. Astrology and bad air were mainstream natural philosophy, not superstition. Others found human culprits. Jews were accused of poisoning wells, tortured into confessions and killed across Germany; in Strasbourg on 14 February 1349 about two thousand were burned on a wooden platform in their own cemetery.

Medicine had no answer. Guy de Chauliac, the pope's physician at Avignon, wrote that the mortality "rendered doctors useless." The lasting responses would be administrative rather than medical. The Black Death was only the first wave of a second plague pandemic that kept returning for some 500 years, into the early 19th century.

title: Quarantine is invented

confidence.note: The Ragusan ordinance survives in the council's register, the Liber viridis, and is dated 27 July 1377. Its effectiveness is harder to judge: the city still suffered plague in the following decades.

people: Mirko Dražen Grmek, Croatian historian of medicine who established Dubrovnik's priority
summary: In 1377 the Adriatic port of Ragusa made travelers from plague zones wait a month before entering. Venice later stretched it to forty days and gave the world a word.
body: On 27 July 1377 the Great Council of Ragusa, a trading republic on the Adriatic, passed an ordinance whose title states the rule: *Veniens de locis pestiferis non intret Ragusinum vel districtum*, whoever comes from plague-stricken places shall not enter Ragusa or its territory. Arrivals had to spend a month in isolation first. Townspeople who visited them, or brought them food without authorization, had to stay a month too. Earlier cities had expelled or walled up the sick; in 1348 Milan's archbishop had the first three plague houses boarded up with everyone inside. Ragusa's isolation was temporary, which kept the port open to trade. Its councillors consulted no physicians and had no theory of contagion, only hard experience.

The system grew. Ragusa set up a standing health office by 1397, and Venice opened the first permanent plague hospital, or lazaretto, on the island of Santa Maria di Nazareth in 1423. In the mid-15th century Venice lengthened the wait from 30 to 40 days, *quaranta*, which gave quarantine its name.

myth.record: Venice gave quarantine its 40-day length and its name, but the earliest known ordinance imposing temporary isolation on arrivals is Ragusa's of 1377, as Mirko Grmek showed in the late 1970s.

title: Guy de Chauliac's Great Surgery

confidence.note: The completion date of 1363 is given consistently by historians, and Guy's own words survive in his book. His birth and death dates are less certain, given variously as c. 1290–1300 and 1368–1370.

people: Guy de Chauliac (c. 1300–c. 1368), surgeon and papal physician
summary: The pope's physician stayed in plague-stricken Avignon, caught the disease, survived, and wrote the surgical textbook Europe used for three centuries.
body: When plague reached Avignon in January 1348, Guy de Chauliac, educated at Montpellier and Bologna, was physician to Pope Clement VI. Some doctors fled; Guy wrote that "in order to avoid a bad reputation" he did not dare leave, then caught the disease and lay ill for nearly six weeks with a swelling in his groin. In 1363 he finished his *Chirurgia magna* (Great Surgery), blending Greek and Arabic authorities with his own experience, including ways of tying off bleeding vessels. Translated into several vernaculars, among them Middle English, it remained a standard surgical text for three centuries.
